home: Every chair at the table has been pulled out a few inches, as if the house were expecting guests. Four places are laid. {v} lived alone.
The bed is made, and the pillow holds a dent the shape of a head. {v} was found nowhere near it. The sheet is still warm to the back of your hand, which it cannot be.
The family photographs have all been turned to look at the door. Not turned away. Turned to look.
There is a second set of wet footprints on the stairs, going up. None coming down. The upstairs room is empty and the window is painted shut.
The cat will not cross the threshold. It sits in the garden facing the house and watches one window, and does not blink when you wave a hand.
A single line is written in the dust on the mirror, in a child's hand: 'she said it was only for a minute'. Nobody here is a child.
The kitchen clock is running backward, one second at a time. The radio is on, tuned between stations, and under the static someone is counting.
Every door in the house is unlocked and standing open an inch. Every one. Even the cupboards under the stairs.
The tap is dripping in a rhythm you cannot place until you realise it is the rhythm of a person walking slowly down a hallway. It has been doing it for a while. The sink below it is bone dry.

Someone has set the table for breakfast. One bowl, one spoon, the milk still cold. The bowl is cracked down the middle, and it has been mended with gold, and {v} was not the kind of person who owned anything like that.
The wallpaper in the hall has been marked with a pencil at the height of a child, again and again, a staircase of little dates. The last mark is for tomorrow.
All the houseplants lean toward the bedroom door, stretched thin and pale, as if they had been listening at it for weeks.
There is a bath drawn, cold, with a coat of dust on the water. A towel is folded on the stool. Nobody had a bath here tonight, or this week, and the dust is still undisturbed.
In every room, in the same corner at the same height, a small damp patch the shape of a hand. {v} had painted over them twice. They have come through again.
diner: The chairs are all stacked on the tables except one, set at the far end of the room facing the door. The seat is warm. Nobody has been in here since close.
The jukebox is playing something with no title on the display. The song is slow and very old and you can almost, nearly, name it. It stops the moment you try.
A pot on the stove has been stirred recently. It is full of lake water. There is a ladle in it, still turning.
The till has been emptied and then refilled, to the cent, with old coins that are not legal tender and have a date on them that has not happened yet.
The menu board has been rewritten overnight in a careful hand. Under SPECIALS, one line: 'Whoever is still here at 4:12'.
Every glass behind the bar has been turned upside down and set rim to rim with its neighbour, in pairs, like people holding hands.
bakery: The ovens are cold. The whole shop smells of fresh bread. There is not a loaf in the building, and the dough bins are clean.
Flour on the counter has been drawn into a wide, careful shape. A circle with a gap at the bottom. It was not done with a finger.
The proving racks are full of small rounds of dough, hundreds, and each has been pressed with a thumb. They have risen. They are still rising.
On the cooling rack, thirteen loaves, arranged in a ring. The twelve are plain. The thirteenth has a crust the colour of lake water and nobody will touch it.
shop: Every clock, tap, dial or bell in the shop has been set to the same moment and every one is wrong by exactly the same amount.
The bell above the door rings once, softly, as you stand inside the shop. The door has not moved. Nobody came in. It rings again, as if someone were leaving.
Behind the counter, a row of keys on hooks. One hook is empty and has a label in {v}'s handwriting: 'for the one who asks'.
The stock has been rearranged during the night into alphabetical order by a system that is nearly right and not quite, a language that almost scans, like a word seen too long.
The shop smells of cold lake mud. The floor is dry. There is not a puddle anywhere and your shoes keep slipping, as though the boards had been wet moments ago and dried instantly.
civic: The filing cabinets have all been opened an inch, every drawer, in a stair of gaps. In each, the folder at the very back has been pulled forward by a finger's width.
A telephone rings somewhere in the building, three times, and stops. Every telephone in the building is unplugged and has been for years.
The clock on the wall is correct. The clock on your wrist is four minutes ahead. The clock in your head, you notice with a small cold turn, agrees with the wrong one.
On the desk, a stack of forms has been filled in with {v}'s name over and over. The date on each is the same, and it is tomorrow's.
The register of residents is open on the desk to a page near the end of the book. The page has a single line, in no one's hand: a name, crossed out, and below it, left blank, room for another.
medical: All the call bells on the ward are lit. Not a single patient pressed one. The sisters on duty say they have been lit all night and refuse to turn them off.
The bed in the end room is made with hospital corners and a mint on the pillow. Nobody has stayed in this room in years. A faint dent is in the mattress, and it is still warm.
There is a trail of water from the lake door to the cold room. The cold room has a new tag on the third drawer. It has your name on it, and your handwriting.
The wall chart has been filled in with a steady hand: temperature, pulse, respiration. All the same. All of them zero. Dated for each hour of the last week.
The smell of antiseptic is thick enough to taste and under it, faint and clear, wet leaves. Someone, you are certain, has just left by the door you came in by.
waterfront: Every boat in the slip has swung round during the night to face the shore. The ropes are all tight in the wrong direction. The tide was going out.
The water at the end of the dock is perfectly still, no ripple, no wind-mark, and a long way down in it a light is burning. It is not your reflection. It is a window.
There are footprints on the planks, wet and bare, leading from the water to the shed. None leading back. The shed door is chained from the inside.
A bell is ringing somewhere out on the lake. There is no buoy there. The sound is flat, patient, and very close for a sound so far off.
The fish in the ice-box have all been laid out head to tail in a spiral. They are warm. They are, you realise, still breathing, just.
dam: Down in the pump room the gauges all read the same number, the lake's number, and a sound comes up the ducts that is almost speech, the way a river is almost speech.
The inspection log has an entry for tonight, written in {v}'s hand, that reads only: 'It's higher than it ever was. It isn't rising. It's leaning.'
The spillway is dry and yet the concrete is wet in a long dark fan down to the water, as if something very large had come up out of it and gone in again.
Every light in the control room has been switched off at the wall. The displays glow green with no power in them and show the dam from a camera that does not exist.
studio: The ON AIR light is lit. The board is dead. Through the headphones on the desk, very faintly, a voice reads the weather for a day that has not happened.
On the tape machine the reel is turning with no tape on it. The logbook beside it has a final line: 'a caller at 4:12, no name, just breathing, then my name.'
The microphone has been turned to face the empty chair. The chair has been turned to face the corner. In the corner, someone has left the radio playing its own static to itself.
theatre: The ghost light is lit on the stage, and in its circle somebody has set out a single chair. In the house, row F, every seat is down, as if the whole audience had just stood up to leave.
The curtain is moving, slowly, though the building is sealed. When it stops, the stage is a different size than it was.
A prompt book lies open on the prompt desk and every cue is marked: LIGHTS OUT, then a line number, then the name of someone in the town. The last cue is {v}'s.
chapel: The hymn board shows a hymn number that is not in the book. Every candle in the nave has burned down to exactly the same stub. The pews all face the lake window, the wrong way.
All the kneelers have been set down at once. In the quiet you can hear them, softly, one by one, being used.
The bell rope is swaying. The bell has not rung. Somewhere under your feet, something with the patience of water has noticed that you are here.
school: Every desk in the room has the same drawing scratched into its lid, a house with a lit upstairs window, and a figure on the stairs. Every one is a different child's hand.
The register has been called already. Every name present. Every name answered in the same small voice, you are told by the cleaner, who is sitting in the corridor with her hands over her ears.
The blackboard has been wiped clean and then written over, in chalk, in {v}'s hand: the same sentence, a hundred times, as a punishment. 'I will not look at the water after dark.'
sheriff: The holding cell door is closed. It is locked. On the bunk there is a neat pile of clothes and a hat, as if someone had stepped out of them. Nobody was booked last night.
Dispatch has a log of a call at 4:12. The tape has been played; the tape is blank; dispatch cannot say how she knows the call was from {v}.
In the evidence room the shelf labels have been swapped: the lake sample is in the box for the old jury, and the old jury's box is marked with your name.
funeral: All the drawers in the cold room are shut but one, and in it, on a clean sheet, a small stone from the lake and a card: 'for the one who comes after'.
The visitors' book has a signature for every day this week, in the same neat hand, and the hand is {v}'s.
The lilies are fresh. They are all facing the wall. Someone has come in and told them, quietly, not to look.
hall: The folding chairs have been set out in rows for a meeting nobody has called. Every seat has a name card on it. Every name is a resident of Little Mercy. One chair at the front is empty, and its card is blank.
The stage curtain is closed and behind it someone is rehearsing a speech, word by word, with a patient, mounting dread, the way you rehearse a thing you've been told you will have to say.
generic: Nothing has been moved, and yet the whole room seems to have been rearranged by a hand that knew exactly where each thing should stand. The sense of being expected is overwhelming.
The air has the stillness of a held breath. Every sound you make arrives a half-second late, as though the room were thinking it over.
There is a smell, very faint, of cold lake water. It is stronger in the corners. You are quite sure it is strongest in the corner you are not looking at.
All the lights are on. All the lights were switched on, you learn, by someone who then stood in the middle of the room and did not move for hours. The floor has a clean circle in the dust.

home: The last entries get shorter. 'Things moved again. An inch. Never more than an inch.' Then: 'I stopped checking whether I was imagining it.' Then nothing for nine days. The last line is a single word, underlined twice: 'Patient.'
'Someone has been standing at the end of the garden at night. When I turn the light on there is no one. When I turn it off, there is.' {v} had stopped sleeping in the bedroom a week ago.
{v} had been keeping a list of every time the phone rang and nobody spoke. Forty-one calls. At the bottom, in a steadier hand than the rest: 'They know what time I come home.'
'I have decided not to tell anyone. They would say it is my nerves, and then it would be true.' The entry is dated three days ago. Beneath it, in different ink: 'Good.'
Most pages are shopping lists and weather. Then one page, pressed hard enough to tear: 'It is not what they want from me. It is that they want me to KNOW.'

A page of little tallies, in fives, in the margin of every day for a month. At the foot of the last page {v} has written, small: 'I counted my own breaths in the night. There was one more than I made.'
'I have started locking the bathroom door even with no one in the house. I have started saying goodnight to the empty chair. It has started, I am nearly sure, to be polite about it.'

Pressed flat between two pages is a drawing in {v}'s hand of the lake at night, and a lit window on the water, and a small figure at the window looking back at the town. Beside it: 'It looks at us the way we look at it.'

The diary has been kept in two colours of ink. The blue is {v}'s. The black came later, in the margins, answering. 'Don't.' 'You know why.' 'Come down to the water.' The last black entry is a time: 4:12.

'I dreamed I was the one at the window. I dreamed I knew all of them by their footsteps. I woke up and I knew all of them by their footsteps.' Three lines below: 'I need to speak to someone about the jury.'
The calendar has a date circled each week in red. The dates are all the same hour. There is one circle left in the month. It is tonight. Next to it {v} has written: 'if I'm still here, I'll go.'

A shopping list, a dentist's appointment, a phone number scribbled over a name. And in the corner of the page, in a small steady hand, repeated: 'Don't answer the door when it knocks twice. Don't answer when it knocks once. Answer when it says your name.'
diner: The order book for the last week: ticket after ticket for a table for one, by the window, 'usual'. {v} has written in the margin: 'Nobody sits there. I take the order anyway.'
A scrap tucked in the till roll: 'The man at the end stirs his coffee but never drinks it. He left a tip of old coins. He left it for me by name.'
In the staff diary, one line a night: 'Locked up. Counted twelve out the door. Counted thirteen the first time I went round.'
bakery: The bake log: quantity, time, oven temperature, and a growing column headed 'extra'. 'Eight extra loaves in the night. Nobody here. Someone has been baking in the dark and leaving the oven spotless.'

The order pad for the week has one order in the same hand every day, for 'the usual', with no name. Under last Friday: 'Delivered at 4:12 to the lake door. Someone took it from my hand. I did not see the hand.'
shop: The day book: sales, deliveries, and in the margin each night a ticked box, 'checked the back'. The ticks stop six days ago. Then a single line: 'Not checking the back any more. Whatever is back there lives there now.'
A customer ledger with one account that has no name, only a number. Under it, in {v}'s writing: 'He paid in advance. He paid for years. He is coming to collect on the one day I can't be here.'
civic: The work diary has a line crossed through every day, as if the days themselves were mistakes, and at the bottom of the week: 'I found the minutes of the old jury. The pages are missing. I can remember what was on them. I wish I couldn't.'
In the margin of the daybook, in pencil, rubbed out and rewritten so often the paper has worn through: 'Tell the Sheriff.' The last time, it is not rubbed out. Beside it: 'Too late.'
medical: The night nurse's log reads normally until the last week. Then: 'Room 6, quiet. Room 6, quiet. Room 6, quiet,' down the page, fifty times, though there is no room six, and {v} has never been the sort to write the same line twice.
A page of handover notes: 'Patient in the end bed asks for the lake. Patient in the end bed knows my name. Patient in the end bed was discharged in 1961.'
waterfront: The tide log is kept in {v}'s hand, hours and heights. At the end of the week the numbers stop making sense: the water, {v} writes, has started to come in at the wrong time. 'Not higher. Earlier. As if it were in a hurry to reach something.'
A boat-hand's pocket diary: wind, catch, fuel. Then, on the last page: 'Something is holding the line from below. Not pulling. Holding. It's patient, whatever it is.'
dam: The inspector's notes grow shorter as they go. 'Readings normal. Readings normal. Readings normal. The sound from the lower gallery is not the pumps.' Then, underlined: 'The lake level has not changed in sixty-three years, and it is not supposed to, and I think I know why.'
studio: The producer's log: tracks played, ads read, calls taken. On the last night a call is logged at 4:12 from a number with no digits. Beneath, {v} has written a single word: 'Listening.'
theatre: The stage manager's book lists tonight's cue sheet as usual. At the foot, in different ink: 'The audience has been seated since the interval before the beginning. They are not looking at the stage.'
chapel: The sexton's book of services, in a firm hand. Over the past month the margin fills with small notes. 'Pews warm at dawn.' 'A hymn sung in an empty church.' 'There was a count of heads, and the count was one over.' The last note is half a line: 'I will not ring the bell for'.
school: The teacher's planner, tidy to the last. The week's lesson plans are intact; the margins are not. 'The children do not play at the lake edge any more. They line up there. They stand and they listen.'
generic: The page for yesterday is blank except for a time, 4:12, circled so hard that the paper has torn. The page for tomorrow already has a name on it, and the name is {v}'s own.
Folded small and tucked into the back: 'If you are reading this, I was right about the quiet. Don't trust the quiet. It is not the absence of something. It is something holding still.'
{v}'s handwriting changes through the book, line by line, from round to cramped to a hand that is not quite {v}'s own. The last page is a list of names. Every name has a line through it but one.

lore: Somebody has scratched a tally of the days into the underside of the table: sixty-three marks for every year, in groups of twelve.
A page torn from a hymnal has been slipped under the door. Hymn 412. There is no hymn 412. The page is wet.
The lake level, on the notice by the door, is written up in {v}'s hand for every morning of the year. The number is always the same number.
There is a bell somewhere very far off, and then another, and then a third that is nearer than either. You realise you were counting, and you realise you are at twelve.
The Hush is a word the town uses for a kind of silence that comes in at the end of the day. Standing in this room, you understand that silence is a verb.
On the window, in the breath-fog of the glass, a child's finger has drawn the same small house with the same lit window, over and over, and then a figure, and then no figure.
The clock on the mantel has stopped. It does not say 4:12. It says the time you arrived, and the second hand is trembling, waiting for you to leave.
Written in the dust of the sill: 'They call it the lake because it is easier than the other word.'
Pressed under the paperweight is a photograph of the jury steps with a shadow on it. The shadow is not cast by any of the twelve.
A glass of lake water has been left on every flat surface, one per room, each filled to the exact same line.
The radio in the next room is murmuring a list of names in a calm voice. You catch {v}'s, and then, a long beat after, your own.
At the edge of hearing, a sound like the whole town breathing in at once, and holding it.

low: You wonder, quite calmly, who last stood where you are standing.
For a second you are certain someone has just said your name in the next room.
It occurs to you that you have not actually seen your own face today.
You count the exits again. You do not know why you count them.
A small, steady voice in your head says: you missed something. Go back.
The silence has a shape, tonight, and you keep walking around it.
You catch yourself listening for footsteps that are not yours.
Your hand is cold. It is not cold in here.
mid: You keep rereading the same line. Each time it says something a little different.
You are sure the notebook was open to another page when you last put it down.
Your reflection in the window is a half-second late. You do not look at it again.
A thought arrives from nowhere, in someone else's voice: they are all in on it.
You are very tired, and the tiredness has begun to look back at you.
There is a taste of lake water in your mouth. It has been there for an hour.
It occurs to you the dead may be the only honest people in the town.
You hear it again, the three slow knocks. You are standing in an open room.
high: The words on the page crawl. You hold them still with your thumb until they remember what they mean.
You are not sure which of the faces in this town you have actually met.
Somewhere under it all, the bell is counting. You are almost at twelve.
It would be a mercy, a voice says, to stop. To simply stop, and let the water have it.
You cannot remember if you wrote that down, or if it was written for you.
Everyone you have spoken to today has had the same eyes. You are sure of it, and you are sure it is nothing.

organised: %s straightens the cuffs, squares the edge of the table with the edge of the notebook, and looks at you with a patience that is almost kindness.
%s does not fidget. That is the first thing you notice: there is not one small movement in the whole body that has not been decided on.
%s corrects you on a small detail, politely, before you've finished the sentence. It is the detail you were about to get wrong on purpose.
calculating: %s's eyes move from you to the clock to the door, and back to you: measuring what the next hour is worth.
%s names a figure, quite unprompted, and lets it hang. It is the price of a thing they've decided you can't afford to ask about.
%s smiles the way a person smiles at a bill. Something is being added up.
remorseful: %s keeps pressing a thumb into the heel of the other hand, hard enough to leave a white spot. The spot goes red. The thumb returns.
%s speaks of the dead person in the present tense and then corrects it, twice, each time a little quieter.
%s cannot look at the photograph on the table. They look at the place on the table where it would be if you moved it.
secretive: %s answers a half-second after the question, as though checking that the answer has not already been written down somewhere.
%s repeats your words back to you before replying. It is how a person buys time.
%s keeps one hand flat on the table, as if holding it down. Something under it, you think, might otherwise rise.
volatile: %s's knee is going under the table like a sewing machine, and every time you say the victim's name it speeds up.
%s laughs at nothing, once, and the laugh ends the way a glass ends when it is dropped.
%s is on their feet before you see them move and sits down again with an elaborate, terrified calm.

organised: 'You think there is a disorder here you can name. There isn't. The town has been carrying a debt a very long time. I only keep the books.'
'Everything is accounted for. That is what you cannot bear, isn't it? Not the act. The neatness.'
'You want me to be a monster, so you can sleep. I am only the one who says out loud what the rest of them live on.'
calculating: 'Everyone is for sale, Detective. I was simply the one who read the price tags.'
'You say motive. I say arithmetic. If you'd done the sums I'd done, you'd have your own coat on by now.'
'It was a fair trade. Nobody forced the other side to the table. They were just slow to realise it was a table.'
remorseful: 'If you tell me it was wrong, I'll thank you. I have been trying to find someone who would say so out loud.'
'I think about the last thing they said every night. I think about it in the voice of everyone in this town.'
'It's strange. You expect to feel like a different person afterwards. I feel exactly like me. That's the worst of it.'
secretive: 'You have it in front of you, and you still don't see it. The reason is the one thing in this room you cannot put in a bag.'
'You want to know what I'm hiding. Think about how many others in this town you could ask that question of.'
'There are four doors in Little Mercy that were never locked. I am only telling you about the one.'
volatile: 'You have never been that angry. That's your luck, not your virtue. Go on, tell me you've never wanted to.'
'It was a moment. A moment, and then a lifetime of moments after it, all just as quiet.'
'Say what you like. If it hadn't been me it would have been the lake. I only got there first.'
